summary:
lunarsite.select is a free web tool that tells you whether a lunar landing site will have solar power and a direct communication link to Earth for a given mission duration. You pick a site (from a list of known landing sites, by name, by latitude and longitude, or by clicking on a globe), a landing date and a mission duration. The tool then calculates when the Sun and Earth are visible above the local terrain horizon for that duration, using NASA SPICE (JPL DE440) and LRO LOLA terrain data.

The tool expands on this analysis with verdicts on solar power and direct Earth communication, and a check against mission requirements (NASA defaults, which you can change). If the landing date does not work, it finds the next landing window in the following 60 days.

This matters because launches slip, and at the lunar south pole a small change in date or place can remove power or communication. The tool removes the need to combine several tools and raw data for a first check, and gives the answer in seconds. And when you want to compare several sites side by side against the same requirements, lunarsite.select covers this as well.
details:
What does it do?

lunarsite.select answers two questions for a point on the Moon and a mission period: can a solar array see the Sun, and can an antenna see Earth?

How does it work?

In its simplest form, it works as follows:

  1. Pick a point. You can:
    1. select one of 24 curated sites (15 past landings, the 7 Artemis III candidate regions and 2 planned NASA CLPS sites),
    2. search 9,087 official lunar feature names,
    3. type coordinates, or
    4. click the 3D globe.
  2. (optional) Adjust the point. The "site map" gives a zoomed-in view of the point on NASA Moon Trek images, with arrows to the Sun and Earth. At the south pole and at several landing sites, it switches to high-resolution LRO Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) mosaics when you zoom in. Near the south pole, it also has a slope layer and two linked maps of NASA's long-term sunlight and Earth visibility. For each south-pole site in the list, "Best points in this site" gives the 5 points with the most long-term sunlight and Earth visibility (NASA PGDA maps), with a slope under 15°.
  3. Set the period. A UTC start, a duration of up to 400 days.
  4. Set the observer height. It helps reflect the height of an antenna or a solar panel.
  5. Read the Verdict. Plain-language ratings for solar power, the radio link to Earth, and both together, and pass/fail checks against NASA mission requirements: at most 50 h of darkness (VIPER planning), sunlight for 6.5 days from landing (Artemis), and at least 25 % Earth visibility (Artemis HLS). The user can change the limits. If the date fails, "Next landing window" searches the next 60 days, and one click sets the new start.
  6. Look deeper and compare. The Details tab has the Sun and Earth positions now, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, a sky plot with the terrain horizon, and all events. You can save a search and compare up to 4 searches side by side, with their verdicts, mission requirements and site images.

Under the hood. A Python API calculates the geometry with NASA NAIF SPICE and the JPL DE440 ephemeris, which includes libration. South of about 65° S, it calculates the terrain horizon of the point from LRO LOLA elevation data (20 m and 120 m per pixel): every 0.5° of azimuth, along 150 km, with the curvature of the Moon. It finds each sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset to 1 second. At six test times, our Sun and Earth directions agree with JPL Horizons to within 4.5 × 10⁻⁷°.

Example. We assume an Artemis IV landing at Malapert Massif best point 1 on 10 January 2028, for 6.5 days (NASA has not chosen a region or a date). It meets 3 of 3 requirements (longest darkness allowed, longest sunlight and minimum Earth visibility). The launch slips 12 days: now the Sun is down at the landing, and the point meets 1 of 3. The tool suggests the next landing window at the same point, 3 to 8 February. In the comparison, de Gerlache Rim, nearer the pole, also meets 3 of 3 on the new date, but Earth is visible only 49 % of the stay, so the crew may need a relay satellite.

What benefits does it have?

  • Answers in seconds that today need several detailed tools (QuickMap, Moon Trek, JPL Horizons) and raw data.
  • The real terrain horizon, not a flat one. Near the pole, a move of about 1 km can change a week from full sunlight to full darkness.
  • NASA requirements and the next landing window, not only numbers.
  • One screen for experts and the public: the Verdict for everyone, the Details for planners.
  • Free, in any browser. No account, no cookies.

What is the intended impact?

Mission teams can make a fast first check when a launch slips or a site changes, and see at once which dates and points still work. Teachers and students can see why the lunar south pole is difficult: the Sun and Earth skim the horizon, and a ridge or a few days can change everything. Next, the tool can analyse a whole region for a period, and help to plan rover routes between "safe havens" with short nights, for missions such as NASA's VIPER rover.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did we use?

TypeScript, three.js, OpenLayers and Vite for the web app. Python, FastAPI, SpiceyPy (NASA NAIF CSPICE), NumPy and Rasterio for the API and the calculations. Google Cloud Run, Cloud Build and Cloud Storage for hosting. pytest and Playwright for tests. Claude Code (Anthropic) for AI-assisted development, under the developer's direction and review. No special hardware.

How is the project creative?

  • It turns ephemeris and terrain data into a decision: a verdict, pass/fail requirements, and a suggested next landing window with a "Use this start" button.
  • It joins NASA's long-term illumination maps with an exact calculation: the maps propose the best points in a site, and the tool then checks each point for the real dates.
  • It shows the problem visually: two linked maps of sunlight and Earth visibility, Sun and Earth arrows on NASA images, and a sky plot with the terrain horizon.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accuracy: the JPL DE440 ephemeris with libration, the real LOLA terrain, independent checks against JPL Horizons, and the data sources of each result.
  • Honesty: the rating is labelled as our rule of thumb, the NASA requirements have their sources, and the limits are listed (Earth's centre only with no antenna model, terrain only south of about 65° S, one point and not a whole area).
  • Users: plain language for the public, the numbers for planners, a user guide and accessibility labels.
  • Rules and openness: NASA data for all calculations, an Apache 2.0 licence, a public repository, no cookies or tracking, and AI use stated in the tool, the metadata and the documents.
